title: Ari Shafer Review: Deliciousness – Paul Kalifatidi
content:
The Ari Shafer is a progressive gravel bike, but what does that really mean? Paul has been riding one for almost a year and has his thoughts on gravel bike biology, head tube angles, really long seatposts, and why you might actually like a race-centric gravel bike for your casual daily ride.

Ari Shafer Quick Hits

  • Named after the Shafer trail in Utah, not Ari Shaffir, the comedian.
  • Carbon frame only
  • 29×2.25” (700x58c) tire clearance
  • XS-XL sizing
  • Accommodates 3 water bottles: 2 inside main triangle, 1 on the bottom of the downtube
  • Additional mounting points on fork
  • 27.2 mm seatpost
  • Top tube bag mount
  • Downtube storage
  • UDH compatible
  • Compatible with 60mm suspension forks
  • 1x specific
  • Designed with 180mm rotors
  • Threaded BSA bottom bracket
  • Integrated headset cable routing
  • Can be set up with a mechanical dropper post, just not directly from Ari
  • Can accommodate full fenders
  • Internal dynamo routing on rigid fork
  • Price:
    • Frameset: $1,999
    • Complete builds from $2,999 to ~$10,500 (with build spec modifications)

Ari Shafer Overview

I’m not throwing shade, but sometimes it feels like the gravel scene tries to claim it invented off-road riding. Ari isn’t claiming they did either; I’m just starting to pick up on that notion when I read between the lines on my Instagram explore page. The original mountain bikes mostly rode terrain that is now firmly the realm of gravel bikes. Especially where I live, in Bellingham, WA, the average “gravel” ride would probably best be done on a cross-country mountain bike. Maybe it is time I put my money where my mouth is and put together a frighteningly light hardtail. Yet, I still find myself addicted to riding curly bar bikes with aggressively low front ends.

Why? I love them. I love how they look. I love how they ride. I love how they make the ride from my city home to the “backcountry” gravel trails feel sprightly and fast, more than a flat-bar bike. I don’t race bikes, and I don’t regularly or enthusiastically track my rides. This is a vibes-based opinion, and this review is entirely vibes-based.

Gravel Bike Evolution

The gravel bike phenotype has two distinct sides of the story, two converging branches on the evolutionary tree. One is gravel bikes that take design direction from mountain bikes. This branch includes bikes like the Kona LBF and Salsa Cutthroat. They inherit traits from mountain bikes, such as boost spacing, mountain bike head tube angles, and 100mm suspension forks. The other branch contains gravel bikes evolved from road bikes. They retain road-bike chainring clearance and aggressively low cockpits meant for high-speed efficiency, and narrower q-factors. This branch includes most gravel bikes, like the Specialized Crux, Manzanita Whippet, and barely, this here Ari Shafer. The Ari Shafer definitely evolved from the road-bike side of gravel, yet I think it sits firmly in the middle, trying to span both branches. Let’s talk about it.

What the Heck Is Progress?

The Ari Shafer is quite progressive, but what does that actually mean? A “progressive” bike design from ten years ago certainly doesn’t resemble one from today, which I guess is the whole point: we progress past what once was. In my opinion, the current “progressive” gravel bike in the year 2026 has these qualities: clearance for 55mm tires and a 48-tooth chainring, a headtube angle of 70 degrees or slacker, a large amount of exposed seatpost for comfort or a dropper post, an effective seat tube angle steeper than 73.5 degrees with a straight seatpost, no toe overlap, and non-boost hub and bottom bracket spacing. I’m not even requiring a suspension-corrected front end, but perhaps I should given my perspective after this review.

While my original description of the evolutionary branches of gravel bikes made them sound somewhat equal in length and shape, the reality is that the “road bike” branch is evolving closer and closer to the “mountain bike” branch, while that one seems content to evolve on its own. More mountain-bike-like gravel bikes will probably meet these requirements or diverge and become boost-spaced, drop-bar 29ers with wider tires and smaller chainrings.

Wow, bikes are silly.

Let’s briefly look at Evil bikes and what they did with the Chamois Hagar. Evil set the standard for what an ultra-progressive carbon gravel bike can be. The Chamois Hagar is clearly inspired by mountain bikes, it has a 66.6 degreed head tube angle, for example. Yet, it can only clear a 50mm tire, which immediately makes me think of it as somewhat derived from the road-bike side of things. Frankly, it’s such an oddity that it sits outside the evolutionary tree of gravel bikes, at least in my mind. It’s an outlier that hasn’t been matched.

Why do I bring it up? I think this Ari is more appealing to the masses. That said, I think Evil takes pride in not appealing to the masses. Ignoring looks, I think that the Ari Shafer’s seattube length works much better for a true gravel bike. The Evil Chamois Hagar has a large “mast” to support the seatpost, which some people find visually unappealing. It might help get the top tube lower and out of the way for pushing the bike away from the body during intense steering and aerial maneuvers, but that is not how 99% of riders are going to use the bike. The Chamois Hagar has a much slacker headtube angle, which makes bike/body separation more important, so I do see why the seattube is so low. That said, the people who can ride a Chamois Hagar like Ian Fey, the talented rider in most of the Chamois Hagar marketing material, are rare. I think that Ari’s design, which places the seattube collar only 10mm higher than Evil’s, is better visually and allows a larger front triangle for a frame bag or really large water bottle. Even with a dropper post, I don’t foresee leaning the bike over like a mountain bike in most use cases.

The Ari Shafer meets all of my demands for a “progressive” gravel bike. It easily clears a 55mm tire, is designed around a 60mm suspension fork, has a striking amount of seatpost, can clear a 52-tooth chainring, has a 68mm BB shell, and 142mm rear hub spacing. All of this adds up to one of the more interesting gravel bikes out there. The geometry is race-like, with a fairly low cockpit, which we will discuss in more detail below.

This is perfect for the “gravel” ride I do most often: a sub-two-hour sprint that takes me across Bellingham on asphalt, onto a gravel rail-to-trail, climbs a fire road, and descends on singletrack. I have found that bikes with taller stack heights feel far too upright for such an intense effort, and bikes with narrower tires just don’t feel suited to the off-road terrain. This is the best bike I have found for this ride, and maybe that is why I burned through a set of brake pads and a chain during the review period. Most review bikes go back to the company they came from without any replacement wear items, but I rode the Shafer so much I had to replace things. That says a lot.

Ari Shafer Geometry

At first glance, the Ari Shafer seems like a geometric oddity. In reality, it’s not too dissimilar from what most of us expect from a gravel bike. It’s a bit slacker, has a more exposed seatpost, and is a bit longer. The stem isn’t super short, so it still steers like most gravel bikes. I used the provided 70mm stem and had no desire for anything different. I’m going to say something controversial: 69 degrees is the best headtube angle for an off-road gravel bike.

I’ve ridden slacker, and the quick steering feel that makes riding flat terrain enjoyable somewhat disappears. I’ve ridden steeper, and things get a bit spicy too quickly off-road. Again, these are simply my opinions. If most of your riding is on typical gravel roads, flatter and less rocky, you’ll probably find this head tube angle more than enough for handling the rough stuff. I think this headtube angle also pairs better with the suspension fork; the travel of the fork more closely aligns with the angle of the fork.

I also appreciate the 74-degree seat tube angle. It makes long, fire road climbs more comfortable. Ari provides a zero setback seatpost (which, by the way, is simple and very well made), and with my 750mm saddle height, the effective seat tube angle comes out to ~73.5 degrees. That’s great for me.

The chainstays are short, which I like on pretty much all my bikes. Ari makes the chainstay length proportional across all sizes. A size small has a 425mm chainstay and a size XL has a 440mm chainstay. It’s shocking how few bikes do this; for example, I’m waiting for an Open Wide 2.0 to arrive in the mail, and all of the frame sizes have identical chainstay lengths. Is that bad? No, but it does mean that the different sizes will handle with more variety than the designers likely intended.

I want to briefly discuss the stack height. Unlike John and Spencer, who will argue that most people should be riding taller front ends, I much prefer being low. Even on a mountain bike, I detest having my handlebars much higher than my saddle height. I live for the climbs and intense efforts as much as I do a descent and a pleasant pedal, and find that I can do more of this with less stack. A good example is my own Northern Frameworks drop-bar MTB. It’s somewhat similar to the Ari in many ways, but one of the biggest differences is that the cockpit is much higher (619mm vs 585mm), a design element I chose to prioritize comfort on long rides over intense pedaling efforts. When I do take that bike on more “spirited” fast rides, I am constantly scrunched over the handlebars with bent arms, and I finish the ride with tired triceps. I find bikes with lower, more “race” cockpits suit my average ride better than the longer, slower ones I do less often. They’re more fun for the rides that I intend to be fun. The Ari has a certified “race-like” low front end. It’s not the lowest out there, but it certainly isn’t tall.

The Build Kit

Ari sent me the “Shafer Comp” build kit, which uses the SRAM Apex Eagle hydraulic drivetrain. I cannot say enough good things about this groupset; it’s affordable, capable, and comfortable. We used to have to rely on third-party modifications to combine mechanical 12-speed mountain bike gearing with drop bars, but SRAM released this and made those modifications unnecessary. It is also not reliant on SRAM’s direct mount system and can be equipped on bikes that do not have a UDH derailleur hanger interface. The hydraulic brake hoods are very comfortable, and the brakes are powerful. It’s a stellar drivetrain that I don’t think gets enough love, as it’s been overshadowed by electronic systems and the hangarless derailleurs.

The best part about every Shafer, regardless of the tier you choose, is that it can fit 180mm rotors. I cannot stress this enough: I hate small rotors. A large rotor adds marginal weight, while it provides immeasurable stopping power and longevity. I had an interesting discussion with my friend Erik Binggeser, who has been on a four-year North American bike tour. He uses 160mm rotors on his 200-ish-pound cargo bike with no issue. The difference: he doesn’t use his brakes much. Most of his riding is on roads where the natural angle of things controls his speed. That is not the case on my gravel terrain, where I am either constantly feathering the brake on singletrack or grabbing handfuls of it while approaching a downhill corner on a fire road. I cook 160mm rotors consistently. Ari, thanks for making a flat-mount off-road bike that fits 180mm rotors without any silliness.

I did opt for one upgrade to this build: I requested the Zipp 303 XPLR S Carbon wheelset. It’s deep, it’s wide, and I think it complements the rather svelte frame beautifully. Unfortunately, it did result in my least favorite riding characteristic: the cheap hub is really clanky. When coasting, the hub is relatively quiet, but a quick pedal stroke results in a loud clanging sound as the freehub engages. It’s a noticeably poor experience. The “SW” version of the wheelset comes with a nicer hub, and yes, it costs more. If I did it again, I’d splurge on that wheelset, but I don’t think you can get it with this affordable build kit. You have to spring for the more expensive “elite” build to option the nicest SW wheelset. Ari, please change that. The people deserve nice wheels with mechanical drivetrains.

On the subject of poor spec choices, let’s discuss the headset cable routing. I’m not saying headset cable routing is bad in general; I’m saying the way it was done on this bike with the provided cockpit components was poor. Ari sent me a bike that is on the more affordable side of the build spectrum. The cockpit features an aluminum handlebar and stem with external routing, but the cables must be routed through the headset. Over time, the cables twisted the headset and migrated counter-clockwise around the stem. I have no clue if this would cause some kind of issue down the line, as I consistently fixed it, but it was annoying and unsightly nonetheless. Couple that with the seemingly incorrect amount of rear brake cable, which formed a larger loop than the other cables, and I found myself consistently frustrated with the aesthetics and experience. I suspect that more expensive builds with integrated handlebars and stems would mitigate this issue. I think this is the clearest example of more affordable bikes having to compromise to appease the expensive side, and that upsets me.

Frame Details

Though I discuss some of these things elsewhere in the article, some frame details and features should be isolated in their own section. Firstly, the internal storage. This feature has become seemingly ubiquitous on carbon gravel bikes and mountain bikes, except for models targeting the ultra-light category. It is not a make-or-break for me. The Shafer’s downtube is rather large, and so I did end up putting a tube, pump, and multi-tool in it. The issue is that Ari doesn’t provide an organizer or sleeve to contain items and keep them from rattling against the frame. I wrapped the multi-tool and pump in a rag to get around this issue. Over time, I stopped using the storage option altogether and was content to store everything in my jersey pockets. Sometimes I put a bar or snack in there, but rarely. So yes, it’s there if you want it.

The door to the storage compartment is where the downtube bottle cage mounts. You can flip the door either way to change the bottle cage position. And yes, when riding with a full bottle on incredibly rough terrain, I did notice some rattling from the door. I’m not saying that this is a downside, because frankly, it was only noticeable when I hit stuff so rough that even my body and the rest of the bike complained. We’ll call this rattle the canary in the coal mine; if you hear it, you should probably be walking the bike anyways.

Speaking of water bottle cages, there are a number of places you can mount them: seattube, downtube, and bottom bracket. I guess you could also use the toptube mounts, but I think that’s a better place for a bag. Regardless, water storage should not be an issue on any of the sizes.

Frame Finish

To put it bluntly: this frame is freaking beautiful. I absolutely love the “rootbeer metallic” color. It looks good clean, it looks good covered in mud, and it has a wonderfully outgoing yet reserved character that is rare. The creamy logo text and other decals contrast beautifully with the base paint.  I kept calling it metallic chocolate, and yes, that’s where I got the word to capture my experience with this bike: deliciousness.

The back of the seattube has a few hidden details: coordinates and map tell you where you can take this bike, and after looking them up, I’m realizing there’s no terrain more fitting: the backcountry roads of Moab, Utah. Specifically, the map and coordinates plant you at the top of the Shafer Canyon overlook. Given that Ari is based in Utah, this is a no-brainer. All of their bikes are named after iconic peaks or riding locations in Utah.

There are some small things I would love to not have seen as part of the paintjob: the giant “M” denoting the size and some silly emblems above the downtube storage. I have no issue with a subtle, permanent size indicator on a bike, but I don’t like how Ari went about it. The first thing I tend to notice when eyeing someone’s bike is stickers left on from assembly, like the orange ones on brake rotors or various stickers that serve a purpose on the shop floor but none to the rider. The “S4” indicator on a Specialized is what comes to mind. That sticker can be removed, but the “M” on the Shafer is part of the paint. For the life of the bike, it always looked like I had neglected to remove the shop floor sticker and make it my own.

The same goes for the little emblems above the internal frame storage. Five months into owning the bike, I shouldn’t have to be reminded what I can store in the frame. The proprietary stem cap that integrates with the expansion plug on the rigid carbon fork is the cherry on top. I don’t understand these decisions, as they immediately make the bike feel more “corporate,” which I know DTC brands like Ari are trying to avoid.

Frame Compliance and Ride

Ari absolutely nailed the ride feel. The frame is quite stiff laterally but quite compliant vertically: efficient yet comfortable. It’s the most compliant carbon fiber bike that I recall riding. I won’t go as far to say that it is noodly, like over-cooked pasta, but it’s certainly not harsh and ultra-stuff like a racing road bike. It’s well tuned for rough gravel. For a brief comparison, I received the new Open Wide 2.o for review and that bike feels quite different. It’s stiffer, but even bigger tires soften that stiffness around the edges. I’ll report more on that in a few months when I’m well-versed on the Open.

The Ari Shafer has a lot of seatpost, which is amazing! Or rather, there is not a ton of seattube. This lets the seatpost act as a leaf spring, helping absorb vibration and bumps. The frame design contributes: dropped seatstays that join the seattube below the toptube and a very thin seattube cross-section near the bottom bracket help the entire frame flex under impact. The forgiving ride feel is noticeable.

The fork also plays a key role in the forgiving ride. The very slender, long blades (remember, it’s corrected for a 60mm suspension fork) allow a lot of flex. With the front wheel between my legs, I could twist the handlebars a lot without the wheel following. On trail, I never saw or felt this, and it didn’t contribute to inaccurate steering. The only time I ever noticed it was when inching down a super steep asphalt grade. I could feel the fork chatter under the force. At speed and in the usual riding scenario, I never encountered any issues and did feel that the fork was compliant and predictable. Funny enough, the suspension fork was actually stiffer (in regard to this twisting) than the rigid fork.

I loved riding this bike. On flats, it felt fast, efficient, and how I want a speedy bike to feel. Every moment hunkered over the handlebars and hiding from the wind was pleasant. The same goes for climbing: I pointed the bike uphill, and it went there. I think some of my fastest climbs have been on this bike as it felt perfectly poised to do so. The steep seattube angle and low front end put me in the perfect position for steep watts.

To suspend or not to suspend

When I received this bike, I had no intention of riding it with a suspension fork. Yet, after a few months, I figured I should try it. The Shafer is one of the few mainstream gravel bikes designed around the RockShox Rudy XL, 60mm fork. Curiosity got the best of me, and I contacted Ari for a squishy fork. Technically, I should state that the fork they sent is a pre-production prototype, but nothing about the ride quality or the fork’s finish would indicate that more prototyping needed to be done.

 

At the moment, I have two gravel suspension forks: the DT Swiss F-132 ONE and this RockShox Rudy XL. They have different characters. The DT Swiss is far more sensitive when in the open damping setting, almost too much for intense pedaling, but this is remedied by how easily it can be actuated with the handlebar-mounted lever. The RockShox is more heavily damped and much firmer even when fully open.

To my surprise, I actually preferred the Ari Shafer with the suspension fork. I typically ran the fork in its full open setting with zero complaint and only reached to lock it out when riding long stretches of asphalt. Off-road, it added just more comfort and control without having to drop the front tire to pressures that handled high-speed asphalt descents poorly. As expected, it made the bike more capable.

Yet, I don’t think that the rigid fork is a poor spec choice. Truthfully, I’d take both if that were an option. If you ride lots of singletrack, the suspension fork would be a thoughtful choice. If you’re mostly riding smoother gravel roads or doubletrack, I’d stick to the rigid fork.

What is it for?

To oversimplify, the Ari Shafer is a fantastic gravel bike. I applaud Ari for making such an adaptable bike; I rode a myriad of surfaces, angles, and terrains and rarely felt out of place. No, I never took it places where I’d want my trail bike, because I don’t think that is the point of this bike. I’m not claiming that the Shafer is a mountain bike for your average gravel rider; I’m claiming that it is a really good gravel bike for your average gravel rider.

It is also certainly not a gravel bike that behaves more like a road bike, at least not with 55mm tires. Sure, I pumped them up to 30psi and did a lot of road riding, but it didn’t feel like I was riding something like the Litespeed Toscano I’m reviewing at the same time. That bike has 45mm tires and toe overlap and feels like a road bike that pushed itself to ride gravel. The Ari is confidently capable at pretty burly gravel and smoother singletrack. The geometry is more stable and composed than any other gravel bike I had ridden, which is why I say it’s planted firmly between the two branches of the evolutionary tree that is the gravel bike. It has a low front end and sprightly road-bike underpinnings, yet its tire clearance and confident handling make it feel like a mountain bike.

TL;DR

The Ari Shafer ended up being one of my favorite gravel bikes. It fit perfectly into my universe where I consistently ride a wide variety of terrain types: singletrack, rail-to-trail, fire roads, and city streets. It’s progressive design pushes the envelope enough to be capable but is reserved enough to remain palatable. Ari clearly put a lot of care and time into designing this bike, and I doubt they’ll have to go back to the drawing board for a long time.

Pros

  • Progressive design is adaptable and capable without feeling eccentric
  • Frame is wonderfully compliant for off-road comfort
  • Delicious finish matches the attitude of the bike
  • 60mm suspension-corrected design further adds versatility
  • Affordable when compared to the carbon fiber gravel bike market

Cons

  • Cable routing is frustrating on the more budget cockpit spec
  • Parts of the finish feel too “department store”

See the Shafer at Ari Bikes.
